plan/archive/conversation.txt.purpose: Archived planning chat (2026-10-05/06) in which Grok Bot was researched, compared with Hermes Agent, and the Hermbot container-per-bot architecture and 8-phase roadmap were designed.

responsibilities.text: Session preamble: environment context (cwd = the project folder, Asia/Kolkata timezone) and an off-topic question about a Codex research slash command; answer was that Codex has no /research command, use /plan.

Deep research request on Grok Bot UX, features and UI. Findings: persistent named teammates, memory, shared cloud computer (one per account, screens per bot are not security boundaries), app connections, steering, files/deliverable cards, skills, scheduled and event routines, teach-by-demonstration, group chats and async handoffs, draft review and approvals, voice, mobile, templates and Team Bots. Included UI layout table (sidebar, transcript, composer, computer view, details, library, settings), avatar-state presence, three-level computer visibility, and strengths/weaknesses (reliability, usage unpredictability, multi-bot coordination overhead, maintenance of auth).

Hermes Agent vs Grok Bot capability comparison: Hermes covers research, coding, memory (MEMORY.md/USER.md), skills, cron jobs, browser automation, Bot Mode with groups and routines, Bot Screen takeover, MCP, subagents, model choice and self-hosting; profiles alone do not isolate filesystem; Grok Bot offers managed computer, teach recorder, mobile, drafts, approval cards.

First Hermbot plan: Grok Bot-style product with Hermes as execution engine. Defined 8 user journeys, three-pane UI, three technical layers (UI, product backend, Hermes adapter), Hermes authoritative for execution/transcripts/scheduler, reuse-vs-build table, early engineering risks (always-on host, shared logins vs per-bot browser profiles, takeover ownership, reconnect/idempotency), 5-phase build order and first milestone.

User decision: each bot gets its own Hermes runtime in its own container and bots communicate like Grok Bot. Assistant design: one bot = one container = one persistent Hermes runtime, separate volumes, no Docker socket for agents, native hermes peer / message_agent as starting transport, message vs task request vs task result contract with stable IDs, group rooms need an always-on server-side driver (browser must not own execution), shared backend for lifecycle/permissions/artifacts/notifications, private memory vs deliberately shared project knowledge, bot-specific browser sessions first, Docker Compose milestone.

User asked for phased plan, POC first, no gaps between phases, milestones per phase. Assistant clarified scope (private web app, desktop later), noted Hermes message_agent is limited to canonical Bot Chats so a Hermbot Hermes plugin is needed, kept sharing out of POC, noted workspace empty and Node not installed locally (containerized dev tooling).

Proposed plan v1: fixed decisions, components (React/Vite/Tailwind/Radix/TanStack Query web app, FastAPI backend, background worker, PostgreSQL queues/outbox, S3-compatible storage, container supervisor, Hermes bot containers, Hermbot Hermes plugin), runtime isolation and ownership split, single collaboration path via plugin, async delegation, /api/v1 surface, SSE plus WebSockets, task vs run separation, Phases 1-8 (POC collaboration, lifecycle/chat, files/computers, connectors, routines/events/notifications, voice/teaching/catalog/navigation, release hardening, team sharing), validation matrix, defaults (3 bots, 10 registered, depth 3, 10 handoffs, groups up to 6).

User asked for bots to manage or orchestrate other bots on user request. Assistant confirmed delegation existed but bot management did not; added user-authorized management grants (manager is an ordinary bot with scoped grant: targets, operations, budget, duration), orchestration cards, proposal-and-approval flow for creating/configuring bots and start/stop, rules against self-escalation, and updated all phases (POC now proves orchestration, Phase 2.4 bot-managed lifecycle, Phase 5.3 recurring orchestration, Phase 8.4 shared orchestration).

Closing: user asked to write the plan into plan/ then implement; session stuck in Codex Plan mode so plan could not be saved; user chose Yes start implementing but plan mode would not toggle off; assistant gave a handoff prompt for a new thread (save plan/README.md, implement Phase 1 only).

Start of Hermes Agent docs research: features overview (tools/toolsets, skills with progressive disclosure, MEMORY.md/USER.md, cron with delivery, subagent delegate_task, checkpoints, MCP), tools registry (web, terminal, browser, cronjob, delegate_task, memory, session_search), docs home.

decisions.decision: One bot owns exactly one container and one persistent Hermes runtime, with separate data volume, workspace, browser profile and resource limits.
decisions.why: User explicitly asked for each bot to have its own runtime; Hermes profiles alone do not isolate filesystem access, so containers are the boundary.
decisions.alternatives: Grok Bot model of one shared computer per account with per-bot screens; Hermes profiles in a single runtime.
decisions.tradeoffs: Stronger isolation and per-bot models/tools at the cost of more containers to provision, upgrade and monitor.

decisions.decision: Only a container supervisor manages container lifecycle; agent containers never get the Docker socket or another bot's state directory; mounting the same Hermes database into several runtimes is avoided.
decisions.why: Prevents agents from escaping isolation or corrupting each other's state.
decisions.alternatives: Let the backend or agents call Docker directly.
decisions.tradeoffs: Needs an authenticated internal supervisor interface.

decisions.decision: Bot lifecycle operations: create, configure, clone, archive, restore, start, stop, delete; cloning copies selected configuration and skills while history, credentials and memory need explicit selection; start with Docker Compose on one host, then dynamic provisioning.
decisions.why: Mirrors Grok Bot duplicate semantics (profile/skills/routines copied, not history or memory) and keeps secrets from leaking through clones.
decisions.tradeoffs: More selection UI.

decisions.decision: Hermes owns native execution history and agent state; PostgreSQL owns product metadata, task coordination, group transcripts and rebuildable search projections that keep source identifiers.
decisions.why: Avoid a second competing transcript or scheduler.
decisions.alternatives: Mirror all Hermes data into the product DB as authoritative.
decisions.tradeoffs: Projections must be rebuildable and reconciled.

decisions.decision: Pin Hermes revisions, images, dependencies and plugin versions; probe runtime capabilities at startup and reject incompatible versions.
decisions.why: Hermes APIs may change between versions; the adapter shields the UI.
decisions.tradeoffs: Upgrade work (graceful drain, compatibility checks).

decisions.decision: Bots, not chats, are the primary navigation objects: a roster of persistent teammates, each with a permanent conversation; threads, reactions, mentions, skill references, attachments, queued messages, steer/stop and visible retry.
decisions.why: Grok Bot research: chats are disposable, bots persist; roster scans by avatar; user returns to the same bot.
decisions.alternatives: Chat-history-centric sidebar like typical AI products.
decisions.tradeoffs: Requires roster-scale UI (search, unread, pin/hide) and per-bot state.

decisions.decision: Group chats of up to six bots with attributed messages, @mention routing, membership editing and human escalation; a single authoritative room history and exactly one active server-side driver per room that decides whose turn runs; limits on rounds, time and spending; the browser never owns group execution.
decisions.why: Groups must keep running when the UI closes; Hermes hosted-room vs desktop-relay behaviors differ so the driver is tested against the pinned version or implemented in the backend.
decisions.alternatives: Client-driven group turns; unbounded bot-to-bot chatter.
decisions.tradeoffs: Backend must implement or integrate a coordinator.

decisions.decision: Message UX: structured progress is derived from real runtime events, never invented text; duplicate clicks and reconnects must not resubmit; reopening restores active run, partial output and pending approvals.
decisions.why: Reliability complaints about Grok Bot (silent endings, missing replies, not-delivered messages) drove explicit reconnect/idempotency requirements.
decisions.tradeoffs: Needs event cursors and state reconciliation.

decisions.decision: Bot creation is by describing a role (name, role, avatar, model, capability config), with focused single-job bots recommended; first-run flow covers create bot, connect app, give first task.
decisions.why: Grok Bot docs: focused bots build more useful context than catch-all bots; strong requests state outcome, sources, constraints, deliverable and review point.
decisions.tradeoffs: Needs onboarding guidance since effective delegation is a skill.

decisions.decision: Distinguish a logical task from an execution run: a run may finish while its task awaits a teammate or human decision; task status, delegation tree and results are first-class API objects.
decisions.why: Asynchronous delegation and approvals mean a run ending does not mean the work is done.
decisions.alternatives: Treat each run as the task.
decisions.tradeoffs: More state to model and reconcile.

decisions.decision: Do not claim universal exactly-once external execution; use durable identities and provider idempotency where available, surface uncertain outcomes, and reconcile existing receipts/provider state before any retry.
decisions.why: Ambiguous delivery or crashed runs could repeat external effects.
decisions.tradeoffs: Uncertain outcomes need human or reconciliation handling.

decisions.decision: All application-managed bot-to-bot communication goes through a Hermbot Hermes plugin plus a backend coordination service rather than relying on Hermes native message_agent/hermes peer alone.
decisions.why: Hermes built-in bot messaging is restricted to canonical Bot Chats, so groups and routines would lack it; the plugin gives one path with authenticated sender identity (model cannot spoof sender).
decisions.alternatives: Use native Hermes peer messaging as the transport (proposed first, then superseded).
decisions.tradeoffs: Must build and pin a plugin and a coordination service; native peer messaging used only as an initial reference.

decisions.decision: Delegation is asynchronous: a waiting parent releases its execution slot and the worker delivers child results and resumes the parent continuation; bounded depth (3), at most 10 automatic handoffs per chain, budgets and cancellation propagation.
decisions.why: Prevents circular waits when bots block their runtimes awaiting each other and prevents runaway loops.
decisions.tradeoffs: Requires durable continuation tracking.

decisions.decision: Communication contract distinguishes message, task request and task result with stable IDs, sender, recipient, originating conversation, deadline and status; delivery acknowledgement means accepted, not finished; reconcile an existing request before resubmitting.
decisions.why: Avoid duplicate work and lost handoffs.
decisions.tradeoffs: More protocol surface.

decisions.decision: Manager orchestration: a manager is an ordinary bot with a scoped management grant (targets, operations, budget, duration); managers plan, assign, monitor, redirect, recover and finish work; cannot self-escalate; relationship does not reveal private conversations, credentials or memory; stopping a whole runtime needs separate authority; configuration changes apply between runs; reassignment reconciles the old attempt first.
decisions.why: User asked bots to manage other bots on request; Grok Bot users create Chief of Staff or Bot Manager bots.
decisions.alternatives: Dashboards, assignment boards and explicit handoff controls (Grok Bot judged these add user coordination work).
decisions.tradeoffs: Grant model, audit and revocation UI needed; default grants are task-bound.

decisions.decision: Use Hermes authenticated Runs/HTTP-SSE API (or JSON-RPC gateway) for execution, streaming events, steering, stop and approvals via an adapter; probe the installed version and choose transport per workflow.
decisions.why: Hermes already exposes runs, events, approvals, steering, stopping, sessions and jobs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Coupled to Hermes API stability, mitigated by the adapter and pinning.

decisions.decision: Default one active execution per bot; queued human instructions are preserved, never silently dropped; direct human messages take priority and can redirect the current turn; stop semantics cascade to children.
decisions.why: Matches Grok Bot behaviors (direct message priority, stop cascades to handed-off bots); avoids overlapping work in one runtime.
decisions.tradeoffs: Throughput limited per bot; parallelism comes from more bots.

decisions.decision: Background execution requires an always-on Linux host: develop locally in Docker then move the same architecture to a persistent server; the browser closing must not stop execution.
decisions.why: A laptop-only runtime cannot work while asleep, which Grok Bot achieves with a cloud computer.
decisions.tradeoffs: Hosting needed early.

decisions.decision: Present each bot with presence/state from the avatar (idle, thinking, working, waiting, blocked, done) with hover detail, and distinguish working, unread results, questions, approvals and failures; status wording must differentiate working, waiting-for-me and failed.
decisions.why: Grok Bot design: avatar carries state; users mainly need reassurance, not a stream of tool calls; its product team removed engineer-style transparency.
decisions.alternatives: Verbose tool-call streams; three animated dots.
decisions.tradeoffs: Requires precise state mapping from runtime events.

decisions.decision: Artifacts are durable first-class objects in S3-compatible storage with uploads, link ingestion, previews, versions, originating tasks, search, downloads and per-task access grants; bots exchange artifacts by reference without mounting private volumes together; the conversation holds the final result or a link.
decisions.why: Grok Bot shares /workspace across bots, which is not a security boundary; Hermbot isolates bots yet still needs handoffs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Requires explicit publish/reference tools and access control.

decisions.decision: Library and structured cards: previews of documents, images, tables and code, editable drafts, and a searchable Library linked to originating conversations; revise existing artifacts rather than creating disconnected copies.
decisions.why: Grok Bot shows deliverables as previewable cards and a Library tab.
decisions.tradeoffs: Preview renderers for many formats.

decisions.decision: Private bot memory stays private; shared project knowledge is a separate resource bots access deliberately; memory can be inspected, edited, removed and searched; memory is not an authoritative source for changing facts.
decisions.why: Grok Bot separates role memory and routines per bot while tools and skills are account-level; Hermes has editable MEMORY.md/USER.md and session search.
decisions.tradeoffs: Context must be shared explicitly.

decisions.decision: Skills: reuse Hermes skills; add create/edit/version/import/enable, save successful workflows as reviewed skills; bots may propose improvements but cannot silently replace approved versions; capability catalog pins executable plugin versions and requires owner authorization.
decisions.why: Grok Bot skills are account-wide reusable instructions; Hermes skills update after corrections and can require approval.
decisions.tradeoffs: Review overhead.

decisions.decision: A Hermbot Hermes plugin registers collaboration, orchestration-proposal and artifact tools available in every supported task context (chat, group, routine, connected task).
decisions.why: Hermes plugins can register tools without changing core code.
decisions.tradeoffs: Plugin versioned and pinned alongside Hermes.

decisions.decision: Per-bot toolsets and MCP enablement are configured through bot settings with the model under advanced settings; model providers are owner-managed with different permitted models per bot.
decisions.why: Hermes allows per-bot models/toolsets, unlike Grok Bot which hides model choice.
decisions.tradeoffs: Model quality must be evaluated separately.

decisions.decision: Each bot gets its own browser/desktop; the UI exposes three visibility levels (status, pinned preview, full-screen takeover with handback) via an authenticated proxy to Hermes Bot Screen; agent input is suspended during human ownership and ownership persists across disconnect with explicit recovery; browser sessions persist across container recreation.
decisions.why: Grok Bot design finds more prominent computer view encourages supervision, so three levels; takeover is needed for passwords/2FA/CAPTCHA.
decisions.alternatives: Always-visible side-by-side, modal or floating window.
decisions.tradeoffs: Requires a computer proxy and ownership state machine.

decisions.decision: Browser sessions are bot-specific initially (Hermes Bot Screen default), unlike Grok Bot's shared signed-in browser; sharing logins would need a separate design while connector credentials can be shared via the backend.
decisions.why: Isolation and Hermes default; Grok Bot docs warn shared sessions are not a security boundary.
decisions.tradeoffs: Users sign in per bot unless a connector is used.

decisions.decision: Connect once, enable for selected bots: OAuth lifecycle with encrypted credentials, refresh, revoke and reconnect kept in the backend; agents get scoped tool access only; Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Slack, GitHub and configurable MCP connections; prefer connectors over browser clicking.
decisions.why: Grok Bot says connectors are more reliable than clicking and are account-wide; Hermbot keeps credentials out of agent containers.
decisions.alternatives: Browser logins only (Grok Bot marketing) or credentials in containers.
decisions.tradeoffs: Per-connector backend integration work.

decisions.decision: Common authorization service for all connector mutations: approval covers the specific proposed action, editing invalidates stale approval, standing permissions are scoped and revocable, delegation never grants the recipient the sender's credentials, and terminal/browser paths cannot silently bypass connector policy.
decisions.why: Prevent policy bypass and privilege leakage across bots.
decisions.tradeoffs: All write paths must funnel through the service.

decisions.decision: Routines reuse Hermes scheduled jobs (no competing scheduler), with natural-language proposals plus editable schedule form, timezone-aware next-run preview, pause/resume, run now, history, and defined overlap, missed-run and failure behavior; unattended collaboration uses the same delegation tools and preserves initiating-user authorization.
decisions.why: Hermes cron already supports skills, delivery and pause/resume; Grok Bot makes routines central and manageable in the bot interface.
decisions.tradeoffs: Depends on Hermes job semantics.

decisions.decision: Recurring orchestration: schedule a manager to coordinate specified bots with standing grants, budgets and initiating-user context; revocation prevents new dispatch and cancels owned pending work per the user's chosen stop action.
decisions.why: Extends manager capability to background work.
decisions.tradeoffs: Standing grants raise risk, so explicit and revocable.

decisions.decision: Event-triggered work via authenticated GitHub and Slack ingestion, general webhooks and Google change detection (subscription or polling), with event deduplication and prevention of self-triggered loops; narrow matching rules preferred over broad listeners.
decisions.why: Grok Bot event routines exist and its docs warn that broad listeners create noise and cost.
decisions.tradeoffs: Per-source authentication and dedupe logic.

decisions.decision: Bot deletion, access-policy changes and credential administration remain owner-only actions; manager-proposed bot creation, configuration and runtime start/stop require owner approval or a matching standing permission, with exact change and resource implications shown before approval and handling for rejection, stale proposals, provisioning failure and partial completion; every management operation is attributed and recorded.
decisions.why: Limit blast radius of delegated management authority.
decisions.tradeoffs: More approval prompts.

decisions.decision: Capability catalog and settings: curated templates, skills, connectors and trusted plugins with prerequisites and permission changes shown before activation; templates are recipes not clones; usage, budgets and export controls.
decisions.why: Grok Bot Marketplace and template-as-recipe semantics.
decisions.tradeoffs: Curation burden.

decisions.decision: Activity inbox with unread results, questions, approvals and failures; browser push, preferences and quiet hours; duplicate suppression and each notification linked to the correct task; manager summaries link to underlying tasks.
decisions.why: Grok Bot had duplicate/phantom notification bugs and uses needs-attention vs unread vs working states.
decisions.tradeoffs: Preference and dedupe logic.

decisions.decision: Start as a private single-owner app with secure owner login and session management; invited members and owner/admin/member roles come only after the private release; private bots and DMs stay private by default; team bots keep one owning runtime with member-scoped sessions, credentials, workspaces and browser contexts; personal OAuth follows the requesting member.
decisions.why: Scope control; Grok Bot Team Bots act as the person asking and keep each teammate's chat private.
decisions.tradeoffs: Later retrofit of access control into every workflow.

decisions.decision: Approvals come from real runtime requests, shown as structured action cards with approve/deny/expiry/cancel; external writes require approval unless covered by an explicit standing permission; secure input stays outside transcripts; unknown action scopes pause for review; managers collect required reviews but cannot approve on the user's behalf.
decisions.why: Grok Bot approval cards (allow once, always allow, deny) and secure forms; approvals must be enforced by tools and backend, not model text.
decisions.alternatives: Model-based auto review alone (Grok Bot's Auto Review is model-based and not a guarantee).
decisions.tradeoffs: Policy enforcement layer needed in tools and backend.

decisions.decision: Deployment on Docker Compose (dev and initial single server), PostgreSQL-backed work queues instead of a separate message broker, SSE for durable events with cursor reconnect plus WebSockets for computer and voice transport, pinned images, containerized dev tooling because Node is not installed locally.
decisions.why: Keep infrastructure minimal for the scope.
decisions.tradeoffs: Queue scale limited to Postgres.

decisions.decision: Release hardening phase: consistent backups of Postgres, object storage and each bot's runtime state with restore on a clean host, graceful drain and upgrades, correlated logs with support identifiers, monitoring of queue age/stuck approvals/container health, resource and spending limits, extended unattended run and provider-outage tests, runbooks.
decisions.why: Owner must rely on the app daily; Grok Bot troubleshooting emphasizes least-destructive recovery and request IDs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Significant non-feature work.

decisions.decision: Defaults and boundaries: start with three bots, validate release with ten registered bots and three active tasks, groups up to six, English UI with localization-ready resources; no public signup, billing, native mobile or desktop packaging; model quality evaluated separately from UI/workflow parity.
decisions.why: Bound the roadmap; Grok Bot itself caps about 50 bots and 6 per group.
decisions.tradeoffs: Limits exposed in owner settings.

decisions.decision: Phases deliver usable capability, preserve earlier acceptance tests and close only on exit gates; POC is the first working increment of the final architecture with real containers, not a mock; cumulative matrix covers collaboration, orchestration, management, authority, execution, recovery, external actions, artifacts, routines, computer, UI and team access; use deterministic fake providers/connectors for failure paths plus real Hermes/model runs for acceptance; test real connectors with read-only and approved writes.
decisions.why: User required no gaps between phases and POC proving the idea first.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slower initial POC but no rewrite.

decisions.decision: Phase 1 POC proves manual and autonomous collaboration across research/writing, data processing and code/review, from chats, groups and one-shot scheduled tasks, plus manager orchestration with injected recoverable failure, redirect and cancellation, and failure handling (browser disconnect, container restart, duplicate delivery, pending approval).
decisions.why: Show the idea works generally, not for one workflow.
decisions.tradeoffs: Larger POC scope.
